messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociation: I pretend it happened to someone else, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar Haddad is a 27-year-old physical therapist who came to treatment months after being sexually assaulted by a man he had known through a professional sports clinic. The assault happened after an evening work event, when the other man offered him a ride and later forced himself on him in an apartment that smelled sharply of expensive cologne. What Omar remembers most vividly is not a full sequence but fragments that seem fixed in his body: the press of weight pinning him, pain in his side and hip, the scent on the man’s neck and jacket, and the shock of being touched in a way that turned instantly from familiar to violating. Since then, sexual intimacy with his wife has become one of the clearest points at which the memory intrudes, not as a coherent recollection but as an abrupt bodily certainty that he is back in danger.

In the weeks afterward, Omar tried to return to his usual life at the rehabilitation clinic, telling himself he should be able to carry on. Instead, moments in ordinary settings began to hit him with humiliating force. If a patient or coworker passed wearing a similar cologne, or if he felt pain flare in the same area of his body while demonstrating an exercise, he was seized by the thought that something about him had been permanently damaged. Intimacy at home brought the same collapse in meaning. He had come to believe that what happened to his body had marked him in a way he could not undo, and that the deadened, cut-off feeling that followed meant he would never feel normal emotion again. The triggers did not just remind him of the assault; they seemed to prove his worst conclusions about himself.

Those conclusions gradually shaped what he noticed everywhere. Because he felt ashamed of his body and uncertain that he could rely on himself, Omar began moving through the world as if his own reactions might fail him at any moment. At the clinic, if someone came up beside him quickly while he was documenting notes, his whole body jerked. An unexpected hand on his shoulder from a coworker could make him recoil before he knew who it was. Sudden movement in the therapy gym caught his attention immediately, and he would turn with a burst of alarm that felt wildly out of proportion but completely convincing to him in the moment. He was certain that if he let his guard down, he would miss danger again.

That same fear made the triggers spread. Once he started believing he could not trust himself and that his body was now a source of shame, the smell of men’s cologne on the subway, a small ache after lifting equipment, even the anticipation of his wife reaching for him in bed all felt loaded before anything had actually happened. He scanned these moments for what they might mean. A sensation in his hip was no longer just soreness; it became evidence that his body still carried the assault. The possibility of intimacy was no longer simply closeness; it was a test he expected himself to fail.

As he grew more jumpy, Omar developed ways of getting through the day that made sense to him at the time. When his body surged with alarm, he would mentally step away and tell himself it had happened to someone else, as if distance might keep him from being overwhelmed. He worked hard not to think about the assault directly. He also began checking his body repeatedly, pressing at the painful area, monitoring for signs of injury or tension, trying to catch danger before it caught him. Yet these habits narrowed his world. The more he dissociated, pushed the memory away, and scrutinized his body, the more readily smell, pain, and sexual contact set him off. During sessions with patients, body positioning and hands-on treatment became minefields; at home, his wife experienced him as far away even when he was physically present.

Over time the pattern tightened. Because he was watching for danger in his body and surroundings, he startled more easily; because he startled so easily, he relied even more on checking, mental distance, and not thinking. A patient shifting suddenly on the treatment table or a colleague approaching from the side could leave him rattled for the rest of the hour. Afterward he would search his body for tension and pain, and that searching itself pulled him back toward the sensory fragments he was trying to avoid. Intimacy with his wife became increasingly rare, not from lack of caring but from dread of freezing, flinching, or feeling nothing at all. What frightened him most was the sense that this was becoming his permanent life: a body he could not trust, emotions he could not fully feel, and a marriage organized around what he could not bear.

He finally sought help after recoiling sharply when his wife touched him unexpectedly in the kitchen, then seeing her face fall as he stepped back as if from a threat. Omar said he could live with being tense at work, but he could not stand what the assault was doing to his marriage and to his sense of himself. He wants relief from the constant vigilance and the way ordinary sensations now ambush him. At the same time, he is afraid that talking about what happened will confirm what he already believes: that his body is ruined, that he failed to protect himself, and that he may never feel normal again.
